    LoRA knobs: rank, alpha, dropout, target modules, QLoRA

    After this lesson you can configure a LoRA fine-tune: choose the rank and alpha, pick target modules, set dropout, and decide when QLoRA is worth it.

    Level: beginner Read time: ~9 min Prerequisites: Full fine-tuning vs LoRA Updated: 13 Nov 2026

    LoRA has a handful of settings. You can get a good result with defaults, but understanding each knob lets you trade capacity, regularization, and memory deliberately.

    Rank (r): the adapter's capacity

    The rank r is the inner dimension of LoRA's two small matrices — effectively how much "room" the adapter has to express a change. Small r (e.g. 8) is cheap and often plenty for a narrow task; larger r (16, 32, 64) adds capacity for harder or broader tasks at the cost of more adapter parameters and memory. More is not always better — too much rank on a small dataset just gives the model more room to overfit. A common starting point is r = 16.

    Alpha: how strongly the adapter speaks

    alpha scales the adapter's contribution before it's added to the frozen weights (in PEFT the multiplier is exactly lora_alpha / r, or alpha / √r with use_rslora=True). A frequent community convention is alpha = 2 × r (e.g. r=16, alpha=32) — a convention, not a rule: the QLoRA paper used r=64 with alpha=16. Because the multiplier is alpha / r, doubling r with alpha fixed halves the update's scale, which is why people often move alpha with r. Treat the pair together rather than tuning each blindly.

    Target modules: where to put adapters

    You choose which weight matrices get an adapter — the target modules. The candidates are the attention projections (the query/key/value/output matrices from Track 0) and the feed-forward (MLP) layers. The original 2021 LoRA paper adapted only the query and value projections, and that minimal choice is still common. Later work found it under-fits: the QLoRA paper (Dettmers et al. 2023) needed LoRA on all linear layers to match full fine-tuning, and a 2025 LoRA study ("LoRA Without Regret") found attention-only LoRA clearly behind MLP-only. Start from target_modules="all-linear"; treat q/v as the cheaper option when memory is tight on a large model. BrewSLM's default, auto, does exactly this: all linear layers for models up to 2B parameters, q/v above, because q/v alone under-fit SmolLM2-135M and Qwen2.5-1.5B in its own runs.

    Dropout: light regularization

    LoRA dropout randomly zeroes some of the adapter's input during training (PEFT computes lora_B(lora_A(dropout(x)))), a mild regularizer that helps avoid overfitting on small datasets. A small value like 0.05 is typical; raise it slightly if you see overfitting, lower it toward 0 for larger datasets.

    QLoRA: LoRA on a quantized base

    QLoRA shrinks memory further by quantizing the frozen base model — storing its weights in 4 bits instead of 16 — while still training a normal LoRA adapter on top. Since the base is frozen anyway, quantizing it costs little quality and cuts the quantized layers' memory to about a quarter, letting you fine-tune a model that wouldn't otherwise fit. Embeddings, the output head and norms usually stay in 16-bit, so small models save less (in SmolLM2-135M the tied embedding alone is about a fifth of the parameters; the memory table in the next lesson has the per-parameter figures). The trade is noticeably slower steps, since weights are dequantized on every matmul, and a small quality risk. Reach for QLoRA when memory is the binding constraint.

    To see what the rank, the target modules and a 4-bit base do to a particular model's memory, try them in the fine-tuning memory calculator.

    Sensible starting point

    r = 16, alpha = 32, dropout 0.05, target all linear layers ("all-linear"), a 16-bit base if it fits (QLoRA if not). Change one thing at a time and measure on the gold set.

    These knobs spend memory. To set them — and the batch size — without crashing, you need to estimate the GPU memory a run will use, which is the next lesson.

    Recap

    • Rank r sets the adapter's capacity, alpha scales its contribution by alpha / r, and a common starting point is r = 16, alpha = 32, dropout 0.05.
    • Target modules choose where adapters go; attention-only LoRA under-fits, so start from all linear layers and treat q/v as the cheaper option for a large model.
    • QLoRA quantises the frozen base to 4-bit to save memory, at the price of slower steps; embeddings and norms stay 16-bit, so small models save less.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    See how the knobs move the adapter's size. Keep lora_alpha=32 and target all linear layers, and try r = 8, 16 and 32 on SmolLM2-135M. Before running, predict how the trainable parameter count changes each time r doubles, and what multiplier alpha / r the adapter gets at each rank.

    import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

for r in (8, 16, 32):
    base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct", dtype=torch.float32)
    model = get_peft_model(base, LoraConfig(r=r, lora_alpha=32, target_modules="all-linear",
                                            task_type="CAUSAL_LM"))
    print(f"r={r}, alpha/r={32 / r}")
    model.print_trainable_parameters()
    Show answer

    The count is linear in r: 2,442,240 at r=8, 4,884,480 at r=16 and 9,768,960 at r=32, which is 1.78%, 3.50% and 6.77% of the total parameters. The multiplier alpha / r is 4, 2 and 1, so with alpha fixed, doubling r halves the strength of each update, which is why r and alpha are usually moved together.

    Key terms

    LoRA rank (r)
    The adapter's inner dimension / capacity; higher = more room (and more overfit risk). Common: 16.
    LoRA alpha
    Scales the adapter's contribution by alpha/r (in PEFT); 2×r is a common convention.
    Target modules
    Which weight matrices get adapters. Start from all linear layers; q/v only is the original, cheaper choice.
    LoRA dropout
    Mild regularization applied to the adapter's input during training (e.g. 0.05).
    QLoRA
    LoRA on a 4-bit quantized frozen base, to fit fine-tuning into far less memory.
    Quantization
    Storing weights in fewer bits (e.g. 4) to save memory.
